connector: We’re nearly at White Sands, and none too soon. Mrs. Spencer brought us a girl when we sent plainly for a boy, and I mean to have it put right today. The child told me the whole story of her life on the way here. I listened. I’ll say no more than that. Come along and hear what Mrs. Spencer has to say for herself.

a.raw: marillas mind was made up before they reached green gables
a.fixed: Marilla’s mind was made up before they reached Green Gables.
a.why: A capital to start, an apostrophe and s to show the mind belongs to Marilla, capitals on the place name Green Gables, and a period at the end.

b.raw: marillas hands held the reins all the way to white sands
b.fixed: Marilla’s hands held the reins all the way to White Sands.
b.why: The same pattern: apostrophe and s because the hands belong to Marilla, capitals on the place name White Sands, and a period at the end. Reins is only more than one, so it needs no apostrophe.

sort.Anne's trunk: Only one Anne owns this trunk. Look at where the mark sits.
sort.Marilla's kitchen: One Marilla, one owner. Look at where the mark sits.
sort.Matthew's buggy: The buggy belongs to one man. Look at where the mark sits.
sort.the girls' room: Girls already means more than one girl, so the mark comes after the s.
sort.the neighbors' gossip: Neighbors is more than one person, so the mark after the s shares the gossip among them all.
sort.the horses' stable: More than one horse shares this stable, so the mark sits after the s.
sort.the girls laughed: Nothing belongs to anybody here. The girls are only doing something.
sort.two windows: Two windows is just more than one window. Nothing is owned.
sort.the neighbors talked: The neighbors are only doing the talking. No owner, no mark.
sort.the girl’s trunk: The trunk belongs to the girl. That is what the mark is for.
sort.the window’s frame: The frame belongs to the window. Things can own their parts, too.
sort.the neighbor’s gossip: The gossip belongs to one neighbor, and the mark says so.

transcripts.welcome: Marilla Cuthbert again. I’ve the buggy out and that child beside me, and we’re bound for White Sands to have Mrs. Spencer’s mistake put right. Today’s question, I’m told, is what I might see in her that would change my mind. Well, my mind is made up, and I don’t change it lightly. Read, and judge for yourself. We’ll also sort out the little mark that shows a thing belongs to somebody.
transcripts.wgrd: People don’t change all at once. I certainly don’t. If a person changes at all, it starts small: a pause, a second thought, a thing done that doesn’t match what was said. Today you’re to watch me, of all people. Write down what I mean to do at the start. Then mark the very moment I stop and think, and ask yourself what I’d just seen.
transcripts.dol: Something in this sentence belongs to somebody, and it wants its proper mark to say so. There’s a place named in it, too, and a place deserves its capitals the same as a person does. Look at the model first and see how it’s done. Then set the second sentence to rights. Neatly, mind. A sentence is like a kitchen. Everything belongs in its place.
transcripts.guide1: Now then, word study. Two word parts this week, and both of them tell you where a thing stands. One means under. The other means between. I find myself between two things just now, a mistake I didn’t make and a child I didn’t send for. So I’ll be glad of some plain, orderly work. Take the words one at a time, and check as you go.
transcripts.morphology: Every word here begins with one of the two parts, the one for under or the one for between. Cover the front of the word with your finger and look at what’s left. Quite often it’s a word you know already. Then put the front part back and ask what it adds. Does the meaning sit under something, or between things? Decide that first, and the spelling will follow.
transcripts.vocabulary: Each of these words comes with its own sentence from the book. Read that sentence right through before you so much as touch the card. Then look inside the word for any part you know. Only then turn it over and check. Guess first and check after, and a word stays with you. Flip the cards as fast as you can, and it’s gone again like a hen out of the yard.
transcripts.grammar: You’re to sort these without being told what the groups are. I like that. It makes a person think. In every one, something belongs to somebody. The question is how many somebodies. Look hard at where the little mark sits. Say them aloud, and you’ll find they sound exactly alike. So your eyes will have to do the work your ears can’t.
transcripts.spelling: More than one, or belonging to? That’s today’s question, and it matters more than people think. I’ve seen grown people get it wrong on a shop sign. Before you drop a word into its column, ask whether anything in it belongs to anybody. Then decide. Don’t go sprinkling those little marks about like salt, just to be safe. A mark in the wrong place is worse than none.
transcripts.guide2: White Sands at last. Mrs. Spencer will sort this out, and the child will go where she was meant to go. This week’s word is belonging, and I’ll say this much: a person belongs where there’s a proper use for them. That’s plain sense. As you read, watch the child’s face whenever somebody talks about where she’s to go. Faces tell more than people mean them to.
transcripts.read: There are two places to stop. The first comes partway through, just as something is about to be settled. The second comes at the very end. Stop at both, even if you’d rather hurry on. And at the second, don’t expect a speech from me. I’ve never been one for speeches. Ask yourself why a person might keep their feelings close, and whether that means they haven’t got any.
transcripts.guide3: Well. I went to White Sands to send her back, and I came home with her still beside me. Mrs. Blewett would have taken her, and I’d heard what she’s like to work for. Then I saw the child’s face. I told Matthew she may stay. It seems a sort of duty, and I’ll leave it at that. Now it’s your turn. Say what you saw, and prove it from the book.
transcripts.chapter: Three questions, and the last is about me, so be fair. For the first, I had my reasons for hesitating. One of them I’d heard, and one I saw with my own eyes. For the second, you’ll need the author’s own words about that face, two of them, copied exactly. As for the third, I said it was duty. Whether that’s the whole of it, I leave to you.
transcripts.wordconn: Your word-part answer is saved, so here’s how it fits. All week you’ve had one part for under and one for between. Well, I found myself standing between that child and Mrs. Blewett, and I didn’t care for it. And I couldn’t picture her under that woman’s roof. A word part tells you where a thing stands. What you do tells people where you stand.
transcripts.workshop: You’re building a character today, with one thing she wants and one thing she’s afraid of. Make them real, not just feeling words. That child never told me she was afraid of Mrs. Blewett. She sat perfectly still and stared at her, and her face was pale as anything. That told me plenty. Give your character a want and a fear as plain to see as that.
transcripts.copia: Here’s a plain sentence about where Mrs. Spencer lives, and you’re to say it three ways. Put a when or a where at the front of it. Swap the doing word for one that fits better. Then tell us more about the where or the how. Change one thing at a time, and keep it true. I’ll be at that yellow house soon enough myself, so mind you describe it properly.

notes.wgrd: Catch the first small crack of change: a pause, a second thought, a choice that doesn’t match how the character usually acts.

notes.wordParts: sub- means “under” or “below”; inter- means “between” or “among”: submarine, submerge, interrupt, international.
notes.grammar: A possessive noun shows who owns something. One owner: add ’s (Anne’s trunk). More than one owner, when the word already ends in s: add just ’ (the girls’ room).
notes.spelling: Plurals and possessives can sound the same. A plural just means more than one and has no apostrophe (the girls laughed); a possessive shows belonging and needs one (the girl’s trunk).
